title: Philip and the Ethiopian (Acts 8:26–40)
hookLine: how can I understand unless someone shows me

cards: A desert road, south out of Jerusalem toward Gaza, in the heat of the day. A chariot is rolling home. In it sits a powerful man, the treasurer of the queen of the Ethiopians, a court official the text calls a eunuch.
He has traveled a very long way to worship in Jerusalem. Now he's going home with a scroll in his lap, reading aloud, the way people often read then.
And he's stuck: he can make out every word and still can't tell what it means.

teach.h: DO YOU UNDERSTAND WHAT YOU READ?
teach.b: An angel sends Philip, one of the seven, to that empty road. The Spirit tells him: go near, join that chariot.
So Philip runs alongside, hears the man reading the prophet Isaiah, and asks a plain question: do you understand what you're reading?

teach.h: HOW CAN I, UNLESS SOME MAN SHOW ME?
teach.b: The answer, in the Douay-Rheims, is disarmingly plain: "And how can I, unless some man shew me?" Then he invites Philip up to sit with him.
Notice who is asking: a court official who can read, who owns a scroll, who traveled a very long way to pray. He isn't embarrassed to say, I need someone. And Philip doesn't lecture from the road.

teach.h: PHILIP CLIMBS IN AND SITS DOWN.
teach.b: He climbs in and sits beside him. The passage is Isaiah's servant, led like a sheep to the slaughter, silent before his shearer. Is the prophet talking about himself, the man asks, or someone else?
Beginning from that very scripture, Philip tells him about Jesus.
Then they pass water, and the man says, "See, here is water: what doth hinder me from being baptized?" Nothing does. The chariot stops, both go down into the water, and Philip baptizes him.

teach.h: HE WENT ON HIS WAY REJOICING.
teach.b: Then Philip is gone, and the man "went on his way rejoicing." Where was he from? The Greek says Ethiopia, which then meant the kingdom of Kush, up the Nile, south of Egypt.
Ethiopian Christians today love this man as one of their own first believers. Catholics see the Church's way of teaching here: scripture, a guide who sits beside you, and then the sacrament.

how: Catholics are taught the faith through catechesis: in parishes, adults preparing for baptism walk with a sponsor and catechists through the scriptures before receiving the sacraments, often at the Easter Vigil.

o: the prophet whose scroll the man read aloud
the treasurer from Kush whom Philip baptized
a desert guide who led Philip toward Gaza

games.q: on the road to Gaza — tap the pairs.
p: asked how can I, unless someone shows me
what doth hinder me from being baptized?

s: the Ethiopian was a beginner who couldn't read
he was the queen's treasurer, reading Isaiah aloud from his own scroll. he just needed a guide.
Philip was one of the seven chosen to serve tables
the same Philip from the day before: a deacon, now sent to a desert road.
in the text, Ethiopia means the same country as on today's maps
it meant Kush, the kingdom up the Nile south of Egypt.

games.q: you're Philip. a stranger in a chariot is reading Isaiah aloud on a desert road. what do you do?
o: wait for him to stop and ask you.
run up and ask if he understands it.
shout a short sermon as he passes.
games.why: he runs alongside and asks a question. the man invites him up, and Philip sits beside him and starts from the very page he was reading.

practice: Think of someone who asked you something lately, a coworker stuck on a task, a kid with homework, a parent with a new phone, and picture doing what Philip did: not answering from the road, but climbing in and sitting beside them, starting from where they are.
Then notice the thing you don't understand yet, and who you might ask. If you pray, ask for the patience of someone who runs alongside a chariot.

wordCard.voice: Ethiopian. The court official from the kingdom of Kush, honest enough to say he needed help understanding scripture, baptized by Philip on a desert road. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: Ethiopian. the word the text uses for the man from Kush, far up the Nile.

carryVoice: Your line: how can I, unless. Even a treasurer with his own scroll needed someone beside him. Five hundred forty-two days now.
